article.headline: The Sports Shirt as Cover for the Terminally Online
article.lede: A single tweet does the work of a minor sociological confession: its author has absorbed three distinct strands of fringe internet culture — incel vocabulary, heterodox nutritional theory, and accelerationist philosophy — yet walks through the world indistinguishable from anyone else at a tailgate. The joke is the gap between inner life and outer legibility.
article.body:
The tweet's comedy turns on the incongruity of its three references. **"Foid"** is a slur coined in incel communities — a portmanteau of "female" and "humanoid" that deliberately dehumanises women — and knowing it signals familiarity with one of the internet's more aggressively alienated subcultures, whether as a participant or a deeply attentive observer.

Ray Peat was an American biologist whose idiosyncratic theories about metabolism — emphasising thyroid function, saturated fats, and sugar while condemning polyunsaturated oils — gathered a devoted online following, particularly among men interested in hormone optimisation and anti-mainstream nutrition. The *Peat-o-sphere* is a subculture unto itself, and knowing who he is places you at a certain remove from anything a registered dietitian would recommend.

Nick Land is a British philosopher who made his name at Warwick University in the 1990s and later became the intellectual godfather of *accelerationism* — the idea, loosely, that capitalism's contradictions should be intensified rather than resisted, stitched together with cybernetics and a darkly ecstatic prose style. His association with neoreactionary and Dark Enlightenment circles made him a figure of fascination for a particular kind of extremely online reader.

What unites the three references is their position well outside the Overton window of polite conversation. Knowing all of them suggests not idle curiosity but sustained immersion in corners of the internet that most people would find either baffling or alarming. The sports shirt, in this reading, is not irony — it is armour. The tweet implies that blending in is itself a skill for people whose interior life would be genuinely difficult to explain at a barbecue.

concepts.definition: Incel slang — a portmanteau of 'female' and 'humanoid' (sometimes 'android') used to refer to women in a deliberately dehumanising register. Knowing the term signals familiarity with incel or adjacent manosphere communities online.

Internet slang for a person who participates in mainstream culture and is unaware of niche online subcultures. Used descriptively and, depending on context, with varying degrees of contempt, affection, or envy.

A loose philosophical position most associated with Nick Land holding that the pressures of capitalism or technology should be intensified rather than managed or reversed. It has left and right variants; Land's version tends toward the nihilistic and anti-democratic, drawing on cybernetics and continental philosophy.

Informal name for the dietary and metabolic framework developed by biologist Ray Peat, centred on thyroid health, high fruit-sugar intake, saturated fats, and avoidance of polyunsaturated fatty acids. It attracts a dedicated online following that is broadly suspicious of mainstream nutrition science and institutional medicine.
